rules.answer_text: First time we met, it was pouring rain and I was soaked through on my round. They insisted I step inside for a cup of tea to warm up. You don't forget small kindnesses like that.
I deliver his post. He sometimes asks me to take in registered items when he's away. He gave me a spare key for that. There's nothing beyond that.

claims.summary: Ruth admits she has a spare key to Marcus's house, framing it as routine post collection.

rules.answer_text: I finished my round at three, walked home, did some gardening — the foxgloves need deadheading at this time of year — and was in by eight. I went to bed at nine. I heard about Marcus this morning and it was a shock.

claims.summary: Ruth claims she was home all evening and was in bed by nine.

rules.answer_text: A vial in my fireplace? I use all sorts in the garden. I make plant waters — feverfew, lavender. The ash is from weeks of burning. You can't tell when that was put in there.

claims.summary: Ruth claims the vial could be from ordinary garden plant extracts, not foxglove poison.

rules.answer_text: ...Where did you find that.

rules.answer_text: I grow foxgloves for the bees. The cut stems are just deadheading — maintenance. There's nothing unusual about that.

rules.answer_text: He knew. He always knew. He never said a word to me — not in twenty years of delivering his post, not once. He left me a spare key and smiled. That was all he gave me.

claims.summary: Ruth admits Marcus was her half-brother, that he always knew, and that he never acknowledged her.

rules.answer_text: I was at his house at seven last night. I'd seen the draft will — there was a copy on his desk. We argued. He was immovable. I left at eight in no fit state. I was home the rest of the evening. I did not kill him.

rules.answer_text: Home from eight. My neighbour on the right — she can hear through the wall when I put the music on. I was loud. I was furious. Music until past midnight.

rules.answer_text: Oh, I've known them for decades. I remember them when they were younger, full of fire and vinegar. I've watched from my bench as they built their life here. You get to know a person well over thirty years.

Yesterday evening, around half six, I saw Ruth coming out of Marcus's front door. That struck me — she's usually done with deliveries by three. Then at seven or so, there were voices from Marcus's house — a woman's voice, I think, and Marcus. Sounded unhappy. A woman left at eight — Isabella Reed, I'd know that coat anywhere.

claims.summary: Elias saw Ruth leaving Marcus's front door at about 18:30.

rules.answer_text: Bell family? Now that you mention it — there was a rumour, decades back. Henry Bell — Marcus's father — fathered a girl on the south lane. A woman named Doris Calder. The baby was called Ruth, I think. The family paid them off and they moved away. I'd forgotten all about it until now.

claims.summary: Elias recalls the village rumour about a Bell illegitimate daughter named Ruth Calder.

rules.answer_text: A greenish residue in the mug? Let me think. His prescription didn't include anything green. That sounds like a plant extract. If it's a cardiac glycoside and he had a cardiac history... yes, that would do it. Ninety minutes, maybe less. No visible trauma. It would look exactly like a natural cardiac arrest.

claims.summary: Nadia confirms a plant-based cardiac glycoside in the mug would have killed Marcus within 90 minutes, appearing like natural cardiac arrest.

rules.answer_text: Foxglove — digitalis purpurea. That's the primary natural source. If someone had been growing it deliberately and extracted the glycoside... it would take knowledge and time. But it's documented in pharmacy texts. It's not impossible to do at home.

Yes. The clinic was in the old will. I helped him word it, sitting at that fireside, about nine years ago.

And yes, I am the person who told you it was digitalis before anyone asked me to. I am aware that those two facts sit rather badly beside one another, and I have been aware of it since roughly the moment I said the word.

I could have said heart failure, detective. He had the heart for it. Nobody would have looked twice.

claims.summary: Nadia admits the clinic lost a legacy in the revised will and that she identified the poison unprompted.

rules.answer_text:
I was at Bracken Farm. Called out at twenty to nine to a confinement six miles up the top road, and I did not get home until gone one.

There was a farmer, his wife, a midwife from the county, and by about half eleven a very cross baby. Any of the four of them will tell you where I was, though I would start with the midwife. She keeps better notes than the farmer.

rules.answer_text: Mr. Bell came in at five yesterday. He signed the draft of a revised will. I cannot give you the contents without a proper legal process — but I can confirm the will was in the process of being changed. He made a handwritten note at the bottom. He told me 'R.' referred to Ruth Calder, the local postwoman — 'an old family matter', he said. He did not elaborate.

default_answers.alibi: I was home. I came over at seven for the accounts, like every week, and the door was on the latch and he was in his chair.

rules.answer_text: I dropped the ledgers round about eight the evening before. I could hear them before I got to the door — Isabella and Marcus, going at it about the will. She came out past me like I wasn't there. I have never seen her that angry, and I've worked for her for six years.
He was in his chair by the fire with the cocoa gone cold beside him. I thought he was asleep. I said his name twice. I put the kettle on before I understood — isn't that a stupid thing to do.

Every Tuesday at seven, the accounts. He'd have the ledger open before I got my coat off, and he'd have already found the mistake, and he'd never say which one — he'd make me find it. Six years of that. I thought it was mean, at first.
